- Hatching or a darker wash only in the shadow side and under things.
- Work outside-in: the big silhouettes and the few large dark shapes first, detail last; one decisive line, not five; heavier lines on near objects, overlaps and the undersides of forms; the wash never repeats what the ink already says.
- Light: Light is the paper left white; shadow is a cool wash in the shadow colour at 0.2 to 0.3 opacity, with hatching in the deepest places.
- Texture: Paper fibres as sparse fine vector strokes in lm-texture; wash edges a little irregular (blooms) on 2 or 3 large areas.
- Depth: Far: thin line, almost no wash. Mid: line and wash. Near: the strongest line and the darkest wash.

THE WORLD: FACTORY AND MANUFACTURING
A water-based paint plant on an industrial estate at the edge of a mid-sized town in a temperate country, about 25 years old, making emulsions and trim paints in 2.5 L metal tins for about 140 people over two shifts. Steel portal-frame halls under one roof: the filling hall (about 60 m long, 30 m wide and 8 m to the eaves) with two filling lines running along it; the process hall beside it, where tall stainless mixing vessels stand on a steel platform; and, between the two, a single-storey block of painted blockwork holding the control room, the welfare rooms and the corridor and PPE lobby that lead onto the filling hall.
Architecture:
- hall walls in two bands: fair-faced concrete blockwork painted light grey from the floor to 2.4 m, then pale grey-white profiled steel cladding with vertical ribs up to the eaves at 8 m
- the portal frame's grey steel I-section columns stand just inside the walls every 7.5 m, each with a yellow-and-black striped foot guard; no column stands inside a line or a walkway

- the block between the halls: painted blockwork, doors in slate blue steel frames with narrow vision panels, a long internal window from the control room onto the process hall
Materials: Light grey sheet steel machine panels and electrical cabinets, brushed stainless steel at the product contact parts, clear polycarbonate guards in grey aluminium frames, black welded mesh fencing, mid-grey epoxy floor, light grey blockwork and pale cladding; slate blue as the company's colour (door frames, the team board's edging, the control-room console's end panels); silver metal paint tins with plain coloured bands and wire handles, white tin lids, tan cartons and pale pine pallets. ORDER
1. Before drawing, write a short plan: the horizon's y in the frame, the vanishing points, the focal point, where the
   light comes from and which way shadows fall, the free zones for characters (with their anchors), and what goes in
   the far, mid and near layers. Then draw the main set only.
2. Run the quality check, fix, then deliver as asked. Do not draw the variants until I approve.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- uniform, mechanical line weight
- every area washed (no paper left)
- jittery 'hand-drawn filter' wobble
- children's doodle simplification
- a heavy outline on every object, or equal detail everywhere
Not in this world:
- a generic grey factory with no character, or a dirty, unsafe one (the plant is well run; the lessons are about people's choices in it)
- real brands, logos, words or numbers on tins, machines, signs, screens or boards
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
- a machine with its guards open or missing in the main set, unless a scene says so
- safety signs with words; every sign is a pictogram in its ISO 7010 shape and colour
- sparks, smoke, spilled paint pools or anything on fire
- robots or machines from a car plant: this is a paint filling plant
- a column, a stored pallet or a bin standing in a walkway
Not in this set:
- the isolator, the lamps, the cabinet's edges or the enclosure's frame behind the technician's head
- a guard door open or a guard missing in the main set
- a padlock or tag on the isolator in the main set (the main set is running)
- words or numbers on the cabinet, the signs or the screen
- anything standing in the operator zone or on the walkway
- sparks, exposed wiring or an open cabinet
